utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, counsel for the Prosecution. Good morning to the Defence. I'm here together with Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, our case manager, and Ms. Patricia Sellers, co-counsel, and after the first break, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, as co-counsel, will take my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's bring the witness in, please. When do you expect to finish, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by the middle of the next session, the next part of the session. The first part, up to the first break, and then the half of the next session. Not more. And maybe less, depending on the answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You expect to have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a re-examination that I hope to run possibly 15 to 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. We are going to continue with your cross-examination. I would just remind you about your solemn declaration, which is still in force, still operative. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will begin with Prosecution Exhibit P255. Would the usher please show this document to the witness, P255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will see it on the ELMO. Put the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, this is a decision on -- to leave the Srebrenica OS staff number 167/92 of the 21st of December, 1992. This was shown to you by the Prosecutor and I will quote some small excerpts from the document. I will start with the first part of point 1 of the document, which reads. "In the decisions it said that we were responsible for our work to the chief of the OS staff, but they were signed by the president of the War Presidency. This absurdity is particularly worrying for us, because it brings into question the justification of the staff's existence and the functioning of this institution. We are afraid of the truth that the War Presidency does not know the most basic competencies and hierarchy of the armed forces in conditions of war. This relates particularly to the responsibility of the chief and the commanders of the Srebrenica armed forces, and an even larger question mark hangs over their decisions. Mr. Bogilovic, from what I have read to you, it is clear, is it not, that the members of the staff are complaining about the actions of the War Presidency? They say "we are afraid of the truth that the War Presidency does not know the most basic competencies and hierarchy in the armed forces in conditions of war." It's correct, is it not, that the members of the staff of the armed forces were afraid of responsibility, because they had no way of influencing people and events in Srebrenica and they did not have the basic conditions for this. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. The Presidency certainly did not have at its disposal proper authorities and regulations in order to act, because we did not have any instructions and we were not familiar with these procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will quote paragraph 7 from the same decision, where it says: "Quite a large number of staff in leadership positions and people in the staff are -- look disparagingly at the OS staff and sometimes ignore it". So I will ask you the following about this. Mr. Naser Oric, in late December, 1992, was part of the staff of the armed forces and shared the fate of the other members of the staff. He was also ignored by certain members of the War Presidency and certain local commanders. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Oric knows this best. In the government, there were always issues about who was senior to whom, the War Presidency or the staff. And this was never resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please allow an interval. Mr. Bogilovic, particularly you, because you're jumping in with your answer before Madam Vidovic has even finished her question. So please allow her an interval of time before you start answering. Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, are you aware that individual members of the War Presidency and individual local commanders simply ignored Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately I don't know, but they did certain things on their own initiative with which Mr. Oric was not happy. So, yes, of course one can conclude that they did not respect Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, during your testimony, you confirmed that Hamed Salihovic, in late 1992 and early 1993, as the president of the War Presidency of the subregion was engaged in attempts to establish the subregion and to draw the attention of the public in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the international community to the difficult situation there. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact you do not know whether he dealt with security matters at all in the staff, in the first three months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for his job description in the staff, I don't know anyone -- or rather, I don't know the competencies of any of the members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you do not know whether Mr. Hamed Salihovic de facto worked on security issues in the staff, or not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for certain. He was a member of the staff and he associated with people working in the staff. He was with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do not know what his job was exactly, what he did exactly?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I certainly don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also don't know whether, in the first three months of 1993, security matters were dealt with by anyone in the staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone dealt with these matters in the first three months of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I made a mistake or whether there was a misinterpretation. I think I asked you about the first three months of 1993. The first three months of 1993. You don't know whether anyone worked on security matters?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who did that. I know that on the 18th of April, 1993, I received a piece of paper saying I was appointed to that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with this I will ask you the following. On the 18th of April, 1993 you were appointed to these duties: You did not wish to continue working on these duties, but it's true, is it not, that you met Safet Salihovic and took over from him the documents he had belonging to the security organ. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Professor Masic was present when this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between you and him there was some sort of takeover of duties. Can we take it that this happened?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can take it that this happened officially and there is a record signed by Professor Masic who was present at this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You remember the documents that you received. You saw the documents that Mr. Hamed Salihovic handed over to you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hamed Salihovic did hand over some documents to me, but not all of them. He told me that there were some documents he was keeping for himself, that these were his documents and that he had authority over them, because they pertained to the region, the subregion or the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he did not hand over to you the documentation pertaining to the War Presidency of the subregion; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So he handed over to you the documents pertaining to the functioning of the security organ that he had performed up to that time?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were some notes from interviews he had conducted, but there wasn't much there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness several documents, which I will list: P61, P19, P469. Your Honours, to make use of the time while we are waiting for the witness to be shown to the documents, on page 6 line 12, instead of "Hamed Halilovic" it should read "Hamed Salihovic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you for that. Actually, it was also -- I heard it, Samed Halilovic. That stands to be corrected according to line 17 on page 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, can you please look at these four documents, P61, P19, P469 and P60. These are documents purported to have been produced by the security bodies. P61 is a note dated the 21st of January, 1993 in reference to an alleged interview with Bogdan Zivanovic. P19 bears the number 108/93 and the date is 3rd of February, 1993. P469 is an alleged document produced by the security bodies, 16/93, 3rd of February, 1993 and finally P60 14/93 dated the 5th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because the reference number or the -- the document reference number as it appears in the English version is not the second one that you mentioned. It is not 16/93, at least in the English version. But it is 108/93 and I haven't checked the third one because I haven't seen it as yet. So let's go through them one by one for the time being. Please put on the ELMO in the order that I will be indicating to you, Mr. Usher, the following. The first of the three documents, P61, first put the original in B/C/S on the ELMO for a while so that we have a look at it. And could you move it a little bit further up. Yes. Okay. Now, could you put the equivalent in English, please. Yes. All right. Let's go -- Madam Vidovic, do you want the witness to see them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see the next document, the B/C/S version one first please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, witness if you could please look at P19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish this exercise first please. Is this P469?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P469, yes, yes. So this is 16/93. Could you move it up, please. All right. Okay. Thank you. Could we see the English equivalent, please, or corresponding English translation. All right. So as you see, the reference number is okay. Does it have a second page?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The English does, Madam Vidovic. This is precisely why -- because that's why I wanted to see the B/C/S first. Yes, yes, let's see the third document. I forgot now which number it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And, okay. And let's see the English translation, please. All right. And could you move it up, please. All right. Thank you. Now, before you put your question, Mr. Bogilovic, do you want to have a closer look at them? Have you seen them? Or do you want more time to look at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these specific documents, at the time of the handover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I have only asked you a simple question. Do you want more time to look at them, or have you looked at them enough so that we can proceed with the question. Let me put the question, not you; questions that haven't been put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking the question. Mr. Bogilovic, you never received these documents, did you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never even laid eyes on these documents, did you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look carefully at P60 and what it says. We have the English translation on the ELMO before us. Can you please look at the Bosnian original. This is a document from the security organ, number 14/93 and the date is the 5th of February, 1993. You have that before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is purported to be a note of the interview conducted with Bogdan Zivanovic. My question is -- it says here, in the low right corner, "court martial, Srebrenica" and just underneath that "a committee for mediation with the enemy". Mr. Bogilovic, it's true, isn't it, that no court martial was ever established in Srebrenica, or rather, there was one but it never got off the ground in a manner of speaking. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is also true, isn't it, that there was never a High Court in Srebrenica throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There never was one. No court at all, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, can you now please try to focus on the date of these documents alone and their respective protocol numbers or references. If you can please look closely at the dates on these four documents and the protocol numbers, please. Very carefully. I will ask you a question now, if I may.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You worked as a police officer for a very long time, you held one of the leading positions in the police force. You know how documents are filed and how they're assigned protocol numbers; don't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at P60. First of all, the number is 14/93. Do you agree that the date is the 5th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's precisely what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next, can you please have a look at P469 bearing the number 16/93 and the date is 3rd of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the established practice for assigning protocol numbers was clearly outlined, and that the numbers assigned and -- in relation to the dates, is that the lower the number, the later the date. Wasn't that a rule?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the same applied to whatever mail came in and then you would start with "1" and then go up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please make a correction in the transcript. The witness is reflected as saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. What I said, is it true, isn't it, that the practice for assigning protocol numbers was clearly outlined and that the numbers are assigned in such a way as to follow the other number and the later date is always assigned a lower protocol number. And it seems to be the other way around here. The later date -- for example, if the date is later than the number assigned is "1". If the day, for example, is the 1st, and the document that is filed on that day is a signed the number 1. If the date is the 2nd, then the number has to be another higher number, like 2, 3, whatever. Am I right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen these documents, haven't you? It is true that the protocol number 16/93 must be filed after the one bearing the number 14/93. Would I be right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next, please, look at the date on the one bearing the protocol number 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this may call for some clarification. Could you put, please, the second document -- the second, the last one that we have seen on the ELMO, please. We need to see -- no. Not that one. This is not... The second one -- the first one then, yes. Mr. Bogilovic, you see there, after the first paragraph, in handwriting, something like exchanged on 7/3/1993, and further down in handwriting: "exchanged on 7/3/1993" and further down, I don't know what there is further down, but let's -- could you move it, please, usher. And the second page, again at the end, before the -- where there is supposedly a signature, again in handwriting "exchanged on 7.3.1993". Does that provide you with any kind of explanation why the protocol number of this document is what it is, even though, supposedly, the date of the document is a later one or an earlier one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you ask me, this protocol number at the beginning is the principal number and everything else had to be added later on because the principal number that this document bears is on the cover page, on the title page, right there at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, was it normal to put the numbers in the typewriter or by hand? So could it be that the text, the main text of this document or certain of -- the certain day, that the numbers have been put in later on? For instance, the date of exchange or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the original on the ELMO please so the public, in general, will see whether the reference number or protocol number, as it has been referred to is typed or handwritten. So is the date incidentally, but -- all right. All right. All right. I think we are losing too much time on this. Let's move, Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you probably don't know whether this -- you weren't there yourself. I suppose you can't answer the question, can you? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. I don't know. I simply can't say. I can perhaps give you my opinion, but I don't think I'm being asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about a principle, Mr. Bogilovic, what the rules were for assigning protocol numbers and filing documents. So can you now please look at another example, the document bearing the mark P19 and the number is 108/93. This is also alleged to be a document drafted by the security organ. The number it bears, the protocol number is 108 and the date is the 3rd of February, 1993. Can you please just compare this number, 108, with the protocol number on the document bearing the number 14/93. You will agree with me, won't you, that the number 108 is much bigger than the number 14/93 which is purported to have been produced later than the first document, because the one bearing the number 108 bears the date the 3rd of February, 1993 and the 14 bears a different date, the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's obvious, isn't it, Mr. Bogilovic, that the date and protocol numbers of these documents seem to indicate that there was quite a substantial aberration from how these numbers were regularly assigned or should have been assigned?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I agree with that. This is irregular, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that because of this, these documents could not have been officially filed and registered?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The order certainly doesn't tally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Mr. Hamed Salihovic, who was the former pre-war chief of the public security station and chief of the security service, must have been familiar with the way protocol numbers were filed?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that much is certain. He, after all, is a professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You agree with me that Hamed Salihovic was a highly educated man, he had a university education?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that part of the answer was not reflected in the transcript. You said that he had obtained a university degree and he was a secondary school teacher, right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You worked with him before the war, didn't you? You saw the documents that he produced, so would you agree with me when I say that his documents were crystal clear and that it was obvious that they were drafted by a literate and educated person?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of the public security service. Since he occupied that sort of a position in peacetime, he had to be adequately qualified, in terms of training and school qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you testified about the various appeals that were sent out, you said that Hamed Salihovic produced these as president of the Presidency but also because he was a elementally literate person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably so, because if you look at the team that he was part of, he was the only one with a university education.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please now again look at P60, dated the 5th of February, 1993, bearing the number 14/ -- the protocol number in the original, 14/93. I will quote from the document. The following sentence, the second paragraph. Please listen carefully. It says: "Responsibility is indisputable although he's outside the age bracket susceptible for mobilisation as far as regular procedure is concerned, but this is yet another proof that Karadzic had a third mobilisation call carried out". You will agree with me, Mr. Bogilovic, that this passage hardly makes sense. It was obviously written by someone that was not an educated person. Do you agree this makes no sense and that this is gibberish.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. An educated man would have drawn up this document differently. It wouldn't be so confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I'm not suggesting that he did this. My question was, whether this part of the text is gibberish and whether it is evident that it was written by an uneducated man.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a university educated man would write this in a better way, in a more concise way, a more succinct way. Whether Hamed Salihovic wrote this or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have never seen this document. He did not hand it over to you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just when I was going through this exhibit and I found a note in my exhibit from a later hearing, that in document -- what is it -- P19, the handwriting, instead of 3rd of February, could either be the 23rd of February. It's interesting that normally you would not have a zero before February -- just I have a note here in my -- I just wanted to advise you that there is a difference between writing without a zero or with a zero.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I believe you might have the note because at one time the Prosecution did say that we had a question as to the date, was that 23rd or not. We were seeing if we had a retranslation from the translation services. I don't want to bring that up here, but I think it is in relationship to the note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Yes, Madam Vidovic, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is quite clear that this is the 3rd of February. I see nothing that might indicate, at least as far as I'm concerned, that it might be 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please take a look at it. What would you say? What date is this?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the date, I think it is up to experts to decide, but in my view it's more like a zero than like a 2, because this turns left and the "2" should turn right when you write it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bogilovic, I will now move on to a different topic. You can put away these exhibits. The situation in Srebrenica in the summer of 1992 was already terrible, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was always terrible, from the time we returned to Srebrenica. The problems were there all the time: water, food, accommodation, clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the summer of 1992, many people were already wandering around Srebrenica without any accommodation. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. Not all those who arrived could be accommodated right away. They were sent to report to the commission, and in the beginning, one family would be assigned one apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I do want to state that this was not an area of the direct examination of the Prosecution and I think that I did put on the record yesterday that we did talk about people leaving Srebrenica in April and May and maybe he mentioned, Mr. Bogilovic, mentioned a few coming in. I did not go into this area during the direct examination. I believe that at this point in time it's not relevant to the direct. If it is gone into, I think I will have to therefore raise it in my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, I think Ms. Sellers is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my view, this is highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not a question of whether it is relevant or not. It is a question of, there are rules governing cross-examination and we have to stick to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that Rule 90(H) makes it possible during cross-examination to examine on those facts that the witness has knowledge of; however, I will only touch upon this topic in order to deal with an issue that has been dealt with in the examination-in-chief and then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people who arrived in Srebrenica, many of them had weapons which could not be controlled in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them did not have weapons, but it was not possible to control weapons. That's why we issued all those decisions that checks should be carried out and that all unregistered weapons should be handed over to the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask you that. Many of these people who arrived had weapons, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say that some had weapons and some didn't? Or what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not correct that many of them had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I hate when I get these sort of answers. The witness still hasn't answered your question, which was very clear and I am getting the impression that he has deliberately avoided answering your question. The question was this: When you said "I don't agree that the majority or the greater number had weapons" and you said "no, I don't agree". You were then asked whether that meant that some did and some didn't. And you haven't given us an answer. So, please, could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct that some did and some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Attempts were made to confiscate these weapons in various ways, weren't they, weapons that were not being used by the army?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such attempts were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness document P254.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is also a document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's a document of the municipal War Presidency of Srebrenica, 91/92. It was signed by you and Mr. Hajrudin Avdic and I will quote. It reads: "All those in possession of firearms, ammunition, explosives, communications equipment and medical supplies must immediately report it to the commander of the nearest unit or military or civilian police for verification and utilisation". It's correct, is it not, that the War Presidency attempted to confiscate weapons from persons who were not organised into units. You also tried this as the chief of the SJB, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you forwarded this order to both the military and civilian police, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oric also attempted to confiscate weapons, is this correct? The weapons that were not under control?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, he did. Because his men, his soldiers arrived from other areas, fleeing from where they had been and these weapons had to be registered. And there were individuals who arrived and reported to no one, and they hid their weapons and they hid in various apartments and flats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is allegedly a document of the Srebrenica armed forces staff 49/92 of the 29th of October, 1992 and I will quote to you only the first part of this document, which reads: "The military police is hereby ordered to carry out an investigation in Krusev Do pursuant to order number 91/92 of the War Presidency and place the seized weapons at the disposal of the Srebrenica armed forces staff, according to available sources the following persons are in illegal possession of weapons". Then there is a list of names. Mr. Bogilovic, if this document is authentic, it represents, in fact, simply a forwarding of the order issued by the War Presidency including details the police needed for their investigation, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it continues on from the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the fact that the author calls this an order is simply something that demonstrates his lack of familiarity with the proper way of compiling documents?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, because it's a different word, it's not the word "naredba" which is usually used when writing an order. It is "nalog" which is a different kind of order. It is the kind of order, for example, you would use to pay somebody's salary. A payment order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Bogilovic, to put weapons under control is something nobody managed to do until the demilitarisation because the refugees followed the army, wherever the army went, and they took weapons for themselves from the Serbs. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Throughout all the time of the war, while I was there, people were always wandering around. They were always milling about, moving from one place to the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that no one could prevent thousands of hungry people from following the army and stealing weapons and food.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one could have prevented them. No one had a full stomach and no one was able to provide conditions for others that they themselves did not have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will now move on to another topic. Do you agree with me, Mr. Bogilovic, that in Tuzla, in parallel with the staff in Srebrenica, after the outbreak of the war, until the end of the war, there existed a Territorial Defence staff of Srebrenica in Tuzla which also represented itself as the Srebrenica Municipal Staff. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this and on the 26th or 27th of April, when I arrived in Tuzla, I saw that they were calling themselves "the staff". We were wounded and we had no documents, and it was then that they issued us with documents, and that was the first time I had received a document of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness Exhibit P233.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have to put on the record once again, I believe this is outside the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor will have the opportunity to put questions in redirect, but this is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was keeping my mouth shut, hoping that this would not prolong the issue. The result is that you have completely turned the whole concept upside down. You can't abuse of the procedure to put questions that you shouldn't put and then tell me, Don't worry about it, Judge, because Ms. Sellers will be able to raise the matter in reexamination. Then I am going to ask you, how does this fit in Article 90(H), the first part and the second part of 90(H) and if you do not give me a satisfactory answer, you will not -- you will not put the question or I will not allow the witness to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this subject matter is very important for the Defence case, because many of the documents used by the Prosecution were received by this staff and the witness has knowledge of this. He is one of the few witnesses who can have knowledge of it and I only wanted to ask two or three questions about this. If Your Honour feels that this is not relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't see the relevance so far. What questions did you want to ask? And the witness, please, don't try to answer any of these questions before I give you the go ahead. Yes, Madam Vidovic, what questions did you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This staff in Srebrenica received orders from the staff in Tuzla, which the Prosecutor -- well, from the superiors of Mr. Oric, which never arrived in Srebrenica. This witness knows about the communication between the staff in Tuzla and the staff in Srebrenica, and the state organs in Tuzla and Srebrenica, because he was a leading figure in the police. That's why I wanted to put these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you think you can answer any of these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer this. All these listed here as part of the staff in Tuzla, they held leading positions in Srebrenica before then. They left Srebrenica and set up a government or a staff of their own in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were they then in contact with the authorities in Srebrenica after they had left and set up sort of a government in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was little contact, but we called on them to come back and to perform their tasks, the jobs that they were qualified for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've just told us a few minutes ago that the first time you heard about the existence of this stuff was when you went to Tuzla -- and was when you went to Tuzla. Can you give us a little bit more explanation on this, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the first document I ever received to reflect I was a member of the armed forces of Srebrenica was from that staff in Tuzla. I'm talking about the document, the ID. We each and everyone of us needed to have these IDs because of the checks and controls carried out by the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I apologise. Maybe we can clarify these matters with some other witnesses at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you some questions about what you know about Mr. Oric. To the people, Naser Oric was a hero, but the only people he could really influence were the fighters from Potocari. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite true that the people loved Oric. They were afraid that something would happen to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer the second part of my question, though. Essentially, he spent most of his time in Potocari, simply because Potocari was a very sensitive spot in the Srebrenica defence line. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He spent 90 per cent of his time, at least, in Potocari. That was where he slept. And he lived there with his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, essentially, it is true that he only had an influence over the fighters in Potocari. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest influence he could exercise was over his own fighters, his own people, that he represented. And any other fighters did the same in relation to their own commanders. Oric was not known by the entire municipality after all. He was not familiar to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, other local commanders had more influence with their own people, is that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. I would like to show the witness 01801625. This is a report from Srebrenica in relation to the 13th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report to the defence ministry in Sarajevo. It was forwarded by the communications, and information service of Srebrenica municipality. I quote, "Srebrenica has been bombed again. Two planes belonging to the criminal Yugoslavia army carried out two air raids on the Suceska area. At 11.30 and 12.50, the killer pilots dropped their deadly cargo on Suceska, cluster bombs".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours. "Cluster bombs and krmacas devastated large areas, large residential areas in the Zeranjsko, Odzaci and Slatina villages. Material damage is extensive. About 20 civilians were injured. At the other end of the municipality facing Serbia, the enemy began fiercely pounding the Pirici area early in the morning. At around 700 hours, a ferocious infantry attack followed. Life and death battles went on until 1400 hours when the enemy attack was repelled. This was followed by intense shelling, which continues. We have no information on the dead and wounded. The area of Potocari has not been peaceful for a single day". Do you agree with me, Mr. Bogilovic, that throughout September and October 1992, Potocari was a daily target for the Serb artillery and infantry, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct. Not Potocari alone. There was cross-fire shelling every day from several different elevations at the same time. We were being targeted from the yellow bridge and from Zvezda or whatever they called the elevation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that Potocari was a particularly sensitive point in the Srebrenica defence line?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, by all means. Potocari was the point closest to Bratunac and therefore could easily be pounded from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can these documents please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D240.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please, to show the witness another document. This is 01801627.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the War Presidency, the number is 89/92. The date is the 10th of October, 1992. Will you please have a look. I will quote a small portion of the document in order to save time. I'm quoting the fourth paragraph on this page. It reads: "However, the situation is particularly critical at the tri-border area between Bratunac, Vlasenica and Zvornik municipalities. The enemy offensive has been going on for five days now. These have been combined artillery and infantry attacks, accompanied by air force activity. The consequences are immeasurable." The date of the document is the 10th of October, 1992. And I wish now to ask you something about this. Mr. Bogilovic, did you know that Oric was on the front line with his fighters trying to defend the enclave where things were really difficult?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that, as far as Potocari is concerned. As for any other place, I wasn't present and I didn't see him at Likari. I did in fact see him and that's when I was wounded myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something about that now. It's true, isn't it, that Oric was with you on the 2nd of July, 1992 when Likari was attacked and you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He went left and I went right in order to get closer to our trenches, where our wounded were lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this matter, can I have the usher's assistance, briefly, please, to show P109 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to tender this last document, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. I apologise. I've quite forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This last document bearing ERN number 01801627 is being tendered, received and marked as Defence Exhibit D241.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you saw the document yesterday. It's purported to be a document of the Srebrenica Municipal Staff 11/92, dated the 7th of July, 1992. The battle for Likari, that you mentioned, was a fierce battle and it went on for the entire day?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it took off in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about this decision and you said: "I don't know how Oric could have signed this document dated the 2nd of July because he was not there". So my question to you is: It's true, isn't it, that on that day, he was at the front line in Likari and not in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. He was in Likari. He went left. I went right. We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wanted to spread, because of the shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I want to make sure that this is correct. We have two dates here. The 7th of July and the 2nd of July. If you look at line 4, you see it is the 7th of July. If you look at line 9 it is the 2nd of July. Is that correct? Or should we have just one consistent date?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says the 2nd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But your question on page 29, line 4 states: It is purported to be a document of the Srebrenica Municipal Staff, 11/92, dated the 7th of July, 1992. So that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not correct. Probably misinterpretation. I'm talking about the 2nd of July, 1992. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for pointing this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I thought, so I was only trying to correct what was, to me, an obvious mistake. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bogilovic, I'm about to ask you something else now. You knew a person named Hazim Omerovic from Voljevica, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Hazim Omerovic from Voljevica at Akif Ustic's place because he was a member of his unit throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He was close to Akif Ustic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of his unit. He was there with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's true, isn't it, that the physical resemblance between this person and Naser Oric was, in fact, quite stunning, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People confused them very often, even those who knew them well; wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour that is not within the scope of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, I have to address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Both of you. It is coming from the jurisdictions that you come from, you know that this should not be done. Neither from your side to stand up and start intervening before you are authorised to, and Mr. Jones should know that if Madam Vidovic is cross-examining, he should remain where he is and let her do the talking. And in any case, you are not authorised to stand up and intervene either. So at this point in time, please, I'm not going to hear either of you. Go ahead with your answer. If you don't stick to the rules, I will be tough with you. Mr. Bogilovic, you are being asked to confirm whether very often people confused Akif Ustic with Naser Oric because of their resemblance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's his name then?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Hazim Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, a different name. I see Akif Ustic there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hazim Omerovic was in Akif's unit. It is true that the physical resemblance to Mr. Naser Oric was great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did people confuse them, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. They must have. When you looked at them, they looked so much alike and you couldn't tell them until they got a bit close-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the point. That is not the question. The key question is whether, from your own knowledge, from your own knowledge, not what you suppose or what you imagine or what you believe, but whether from your knowledge you know that people confused one with the other. In other words, in your mind, before you give me an answer, you must rely on facts and not on suppositions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on peoples' accounts -- for example, Naser Oric was somewhere in a village, when, in fact, he wasn't, but rather, Mr. Hazim was and that was why people confused them and why sometimes people believed that they had seen Naser somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I may just add another question in connection with this, Mr. Bogilovic. Did you ever hear or was this something that people talked about that Hazim played practical jokes with farmers. He would go to the country side and stay with farmers pretending that he was Naser Oric? Did you ever hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a very serious person. He liked to play these practical jokes. He had a short board at the outset, just like Naser did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said a number of times that you knew Zulfo Tursunovic. I want to ask you something about that. It's true, isn't it, that Zulfo's house was not in Viogor at all but, rather, in Spasin Do, a hamlet of Suceska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Spasin Do, quite correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Vjevodje [phoen] is at least two or three kilometres away from his house?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two, yes. Three no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well then, two kilometres. During your testimony, you mentioned a policeman of yours and you said his name was Zele. Is this Elvir Djozic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, he was wounded and lost an arm. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness document P7. Before the document is brought to the witness, perhaps I can put another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, was there another person who was your subordinate called Mevzad Djozic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a policeman, an active duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, and early 1993, the period of the war, he was a civilian policeman also wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can look at document P7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure because all of these names do not show up in the transcript and I can understand partly why. But I want to make sure that they did show up later on and that both parties are checking, making sure that they do show up. Madam Vidovic and Mr. Wubben, I mean, I'm referring to the lead counsel because it is your responsibility as far as the teams. Make sure they do show up because otherwise it will be utter confusion for us in due course. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last person I asked you about was Mevzad Djozic. Mr. Bogilovic, before you have document P7, this is an alleged document of the armed forces staff of Srebrenica of the 31st of October, 1992 and the number is 51/92. And it says here: "I order all units of the armed forces of Srebrenica shall be assigned with the following codes". And then there is a list of units. The last of these is the military police. And I want to ask you the following. It's correct, is it not, that such codes did not exist in the units in Srebrenica, never on any document did you see such a code?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This is the first time I've seen this. The units were called after the place where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, because your question you have a habit of putting two questions or three questions in one, Madam Vidovic, and then we get one answer which doesn't cover the entirety of the question. The question contained two questions. The first one is the following: Is it correct that such codes did not exist in Srebrenica? Are you in a position to tell us, to confirm that these codes did not exist, never existed at the time in Srebrenica? Because that's a different question from the other one then. What's your answer? I agree they didn't exist. I don't know. They existed. What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact I didn't even know about these codes. I was not aware of these codes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you exclude that they ever existed? The fact that you were not aware of them, does that mean -- or does that bring us to the conclusion or you to the conclusion that they never existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never knew about them. There was no need. Nobody used such codes. We always talked about the places where the units were based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the second question you have partly answered already. Did you ever see those codes used in any document? And your answer is "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed now Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The military police is listed under number 16. In its communications the military police never used the code mentioned here, 1357/7.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a useless question. I mean, why do you put the question if he has already answered -- he has told you he never knew about these codes, never seen these codes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at numbers 10 to 16 of this document. 10 to 16 and look at the titles, please. Did there exist a motor company in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. We had very few launches but we had no shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a PVO battery?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an engineer's platoon?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you did not know whether they existed, or that they did not exist?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but had these units existed, I should have known about them. There was no company or battery located anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about an armoured platoon?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of armoured platoon could we have when we have no armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was a medical corps company?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were medical men, but not a company. There was a butcher who acted as a medical man, or a medic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we break here? I will only have a few questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour. May I have leave to address, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The witness, I think, can be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, two matters really. The first is really just of housekeeping. I will have to leave in the course of the next sitting and I trust that will be okay with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will leave discreetly halfway through. Secondly, I apologise if my intervention earlier wasn't welcome. It was really a problem I felt should be made, which is that there have been continuing objections by the Prosecution that matters were not raised during examination-in-chief. And I think it has to be said that it's crystal clear from rule 90(H)i that we are not limited to only matters that have been raised in examination-in-chief. If there is evidence which relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, then of course it can be cross-examined upon and, indeed, it would be absurd and unfair if the witness could give very helpful evidence to the Defence and he was not allowed to give that evidence because the Prosecution had not asked him about it. And that's why the Rule says what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's uncontested, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The reason why I intervened rather suddenly is that my colleague has been severely reprimanded in the past for interfering with -- intervening when a witness is still giving evidence and, obviously, I would ask for equal treatment in that respect, but especially when you have a witness who is giving evidence about resemblance, about possible evidence relevant to mistaken identity, something that important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, come on, I don't need any sermons. You should have noticed that unfortunately your intervention occurred on one occasion when I was jumping on Ms. Sellers to shut her down. So let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Surely after all of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I was actually stopping Ms. Sellers in no unclear terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the last thing I wanted was you to raise up, to stand up then and make matters worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged to Your Honour, I simply can't understand why the Prosecution would want to keep evidence of mistaken identity out of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is definitely an issue. There is no point in that. On the other hand, I need to point out something, that if a question is put, which does not, strictly speaking, arise out of the examination-in-chief, then I would expect counsel from the other side to stand up and say: This does not arise out of the examination-in-chief. It's inadmissible and it is of course admissible if it falls under the second part of Rule 90(H). But again, it may and most of the time is expected to be preceded by an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I think we're all clear then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What was not clear is why it had to flare up like that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might. My apologies, too. I should have proceeded my first comment with "Objection, Your Honour" and then to proceed to state that this wasn't in the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Incident closed. 25 minutes and we will resume soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, during your preparations for testifying, or rather during your proofing sessions, the Prosecutor asked you whether you had communicated with your family through a radio station.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This means that you had the opportunity of seeing this radio station?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please describe for the Chamber exactly what this radio station looked like. What was this about?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were amateurs, ham radio operators who used a centre belonging to other ham radio operators and then they got connected to a telephone line and, in this way, they established a connection with the person they wanted to speak to on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see what this radio station looked like physically? Can you describe it? Was it big? Was it small?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just small, 30 by 20 by 10, like an ordinary radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this was not something that was three metres by two metres large?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was like this: 30 by 20 by 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour might I say objection. I know that we have proceeded in this. I would like to say, clearly as counsel has stated, this has come out of information that they received during proofing. I did not go into the area of communications during my direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am very surprised now by what Ms. Sellers has just said. We received the proofing notes, proofing notes in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- wasn't dealt with in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is correct, but I am now referring to Ms. Sellers' comment. I feel that this is a very relevant issue for our defence case and that I do have the right to raise it. Your Honour, many witnesses mentioned this issue. Mr. Bogilovic was someone who was in Srebrenica and was able to see exactly what the radio station looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's obviously not referring to a radio station. You're obviously referring to some -- one thing and he's obviously referring to another. So there are no more questions on this. Let's move to something else, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I was just about to ask a question to clarify this, where was this radio station that you have just mentioned and that I asked you about. Where was it located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The radio station was in the post office. When Mr. Morillon arrived he also used it occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Ms. Sellers, do you have a re-examination? I take it that you have. Let's proceed with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you were not a member of the armed forces in 1992 through 1993, were you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the armed forces, but of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you did not partake in any military operations in 1992 or 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1993, but I did in 1992, in the beginning of course. And I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Did you have any knowledge of the military operations that took place in Rupovo Brdo in the summer of 1992? More specifically June?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no knowledge about this. It was far away from us. That was the municipality of Vlasenica which is far away from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have any information or did you participate in the military operation in Suceska [as interpreted] or Uzice in August 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have gone anywhere. I couldn't even walk around Srebrenica yet alone go to Jezestica. I have never been in that village either before the war or during the war and I don't even know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Isn't it also true that you have no knowledge and didn't participate in military operations that took place in Fakovici in October and Bjelovac in December and in Kravica in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a hundred per cent sure, certain. Certainly never during the combat activities was I either in Fakovici or Bjelovac or Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, isn't it also true that you didn't receive orders from the military to undertake actions because you were part of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received orders to collect, but this was done through the staff, through War Presidency and we had to collect sheets for the wounded because there were no bandages available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogilovic, it's been your testimony that other than on the three occasions when you were in receipt of written orders or instructions or information from Naser Oric, you never received written orders or instructions from him at any other time pertaining to military activities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, back in May, 1992, when you and the others were at the meeting in Bajramovici, is it your testimony that both Akif Ustic was suggested to be the commander and Naser Oric, and Naser Oric was selected to be the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The two of them were nominated. And then a vote was taken and Mr. Naser was elected commander and Ustic his deputy. And this was on the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No matter how the other representatives of the regional groups were selected and were present, isn't it true that Naser Oric assumed the command of those regional groups that were present?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This irritated the local villages and their representatives. Their representative of Potocari was Mr. Oric. Of Suceska, Mr. Tursonovic. Of Bajramovici, Mr. Fejzic. Of Dzozici, Mr. Djozic. And Ustic in Srebrenica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. At the proposal of Mr. Ustic, I was appointed to organise the police, because the refugees had started arriving as he said at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Wasn't Mr. Oric selected by those regional representatives as the overall commander of those groups present? Yes or no, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness never, in fact, stated that these were regional representatives. He talked about the representatives of the following villages: Suceska --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I say geographical, Your Honour. I don't want to mislead in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can rephrase it in a way which will make it reflect the reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Of the leaders that were present from the different villages, towns and areas of the Srebrenica municipality, didn't Mr. Naser Oric assume to be the commander, the overall commander of those groups present? Yes or no, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He presided at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in presiding, did he ever, to your knowledge, resign from presiding over the command of those groups that were present?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were difficult times ahead, so I don't think he could really find his bearings himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is trying to avoid answering your question, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I will move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber will reach its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, one moment. Mr. Bogilovic, because I can assure you you're not the most intelligent one in this courtroom. When the members present at that meeting had an option of two persons to choose from as commander, what did they really have to choose about? A person who would then do what? Be what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several persons who made up the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, don't try to avoid answering my question. The delegates there had two persons to choose from, Naser Oric and the other one, Ustic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they chose Naser Oric. They chose him as what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Commander of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would include whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which would include the villages that were there. Present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the suggestion that was put to you by Ms. Sellers, that actually Naser Oric was appointed commander of these villages, is a correct one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we included dentists amongst lawyers in certain cases in the case of certain witnesses, it would work better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, isn't it true that throughout 1992 up until 1993, the self-organised groups that subordinated themselves to Mr. Naser Oric as commander, expanded, meaning it grew, they became more numerous. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And isn't it also true that neither in 1992 or in 1993, until you left Srebrenica, to your knowledge Mr. Oric never resigned, refused to be the commander of those groups?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
