utterances.text: One moment. Yes, answer your question first. And then we will see what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ms. Sellers keeps using the term "subordinated to Naser Oric". We were speaking about the staff throughout, weren't we, not about Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that we were also speaking about self-organised groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That came under the command. Now the word should be "put under his authority", or something to note that he is now -- has overall command. I certainly don't mind a change of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Try to restrict it to what we are familiar with, but I don't think there is any confusion in our minds what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now Mr. Bogilovic, I just want to go over with you very briefly a couple of the documents that we've already seen and one or two documents that are new. Could we please have P254. If we put that on Sanctions, I don't know whether -- Sanctions in English, and we will give it to Mr. Bogilovic in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the document signed by him and Hajrudin Avdic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm also going to ask that document P5 be shown to the witness at the same time, please. They're interrelated documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you've testified that this document, the document P254, wherein an order, where you say that anyone who is in possession of a firearm must turn the firearm over to the military or civilian police. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You note in this order, you're saying that this order must be carried out by the 25th of October, 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You issued the order along with Mr. Avdic on the 14th of October, 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made, the decision and signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a member of the civilian police -- well, I'm sorry, as the chief of public security service, you certainly can tell ordinary citizens what to do in relationship to arms and to weapons that are in the public. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I believed I had those powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you had those powers pursuant to a law because at the top of this order you do quote the law on general administration procedures, the law on acquisition, possession and bearing of firearms. Isn't that correct? You will have to vocalise your yes or your no in the microphone, Mr. Bogilovic, so that --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Now, Mr. Bogilovic, the order that we've -- we're looking at was not directed -- it was not a direct order to the military police. You will agree with that won't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because that's not what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, you do not agree that that's what it says? Or would you please answer again more clearly. Is this a direct order to the military police --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that it was not to the military police, because that is not what the document reflects.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogilovic. Now I would ask you to look at P5. Mr. Bogilovic, this document is from October 29th, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And this document, the date on this document, certainly seems to be outside of the scope as to when you set the deadline on document P254, which is that order must be carried out by the 25th of October, 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this order 0123952 is not in reference to my area. This is 40 kilometres away from where we were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, thank you for that information, but my question is: Isn't the second document, what I'm referring to now as P5, isn't that a direct order to the military police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "order" here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And it says in the first line: The military police is hereby ordered to carry out the investigation pursuant to a document that refers to your order. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference to an order by the War Presidency here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogilovic, you did not write this order to the military police, did you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has avoided even trying to confirm to you that order number 91/92 of the War Presidency is the order that he was shown before, which carries his signature. Could you show him again now the previous document and he will confirm to us that that previous document is a War Presidency order which carries a number of 91/92 and also carries his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by this order or naradba. As for this other order, or nalog, I really don't know. This order is signed by myself and Mr. Avdic. I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And in the other order that you have, when it refers to -- pursuant to order 91/92 of the War Presidency, what order are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order here named nalog was only made a good deal later and it was in reference to these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, read the second line of that nalog. What does it say? 91/92. And before it says: "Naredbom Ratnog". I can't see it all. But "predsjednistva 91/92". What is it referring to? Is it referring to the previous document that you saw which carries your signature as well as that of Hajrudin Avdic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both these documents refer to the 14th of October when the War Presidency and the staff held a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I cannot accept that this is what you really understood from my question. I will ask you to read the first and the second line of this nalog, this order of the 29th of October, 1992. Could you please read it. And then when I ask you to stop. Stop. Stop after 91/92. Read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pursuant to order of the War Presidency, number 91/92, the military police is hereby ordered to carry out an investigation".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. What do you understand that this document refers to? When it says, "predsjednistva 91/92". Are they referring to the previous nalog that you saw which carries your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, because eventually a decision was adopted on the 14th of October. You have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To take this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, usher, give him back the previous one, 254. Yes. What is the protocol number or the reference number of that document, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 91/92, the date is the 14th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is it a decision and order of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the first part here, it's the War Presidency. But we are members of the War Presidency and, therefore, we are authorised, Mr. Avdic as the president of the War Presidency and myself as chief, we are authorised to issue this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when in the other document, which is supposedly signed by Mr. Oric, there is a reference to "order of the War Presidency 91/92", is it referring to the other document that you've just seen which carries your signature, or not? It's unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be another document issued by the War Presidency bearing protocol number 91/92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the decision of my appointment as well, I think it was also adopted on the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But would it have the number 91/92? Because when you were asked questions as to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in terms of the numeric order. Every document should have its own number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when it says 91/92, I suppose that there can only be one document issued by the War Presidency bearing that number, 91/92. There cannot be another one, according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for the staff of the armed forces to issue an order like this, ordering the military police to confiscate weapons from these persons, in order for that to happen, it should first have obtained approval which it did on the 14th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am not going to ask you any more questions and I hope very few more questions will be asked to you because I am not believing you, that little bit, Mr. Bogilovic. There cannot be such confusion in your mind. You know exactly what my question was and you have been trying for the past 15 minutes to avoid answering it. And you will not be given any further opportunity to answer it now. Madam Sellers, please, if you could proceed and conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will try to go as rapidly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, have you seen Exhibit 150 that he looked at yesterday during the cross-examination. Mr. Bogilovic, as a member of the chief of public security and a member of the civilian police, are you familiar with giving out both written orders in the time you give out oral orders that must be followed? Is that part of the procedure, normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is a problem with interpretation if I read his eyes and his gestures correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand. I am going to keep on talking and when you -- when you are receiving interpretation, please give me a sign, a signal. Are you receiving interpretation? He is not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the meantime I want to -- Mr. Oric, you are not receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a technical problem that we need to solve before we proceed. Please attract my attention straight away when there is this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation now? It seems that interpretation is not reaching the witness and the accused. I will ask again the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, we can proceed. And I lost track now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I believe I asked you, as the chief of public security and formerly as a police officer, sector leader, did you at times give orders that were written or oral -- or orders that were oral and that they were expected to be followed?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered, in both kinds of ways. I would put my orders in writing, or I would issue oral orders by megaphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at the document in front of you, P 150. You have looked at it before. Could I please draw your attention to the sentence that comes under the first wording of "order". Would you agree with me that it basically reads: "Following an oral order by the commander of Srebrenica, that it was necessary to collect 5.000, 7.62-millimetre bullets. I hereby order." Mr. Bogilovic, do you agree that that is what it says?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this before. I can read out to you exactly what it says, but I'm not aware of what it states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bogilovic. You were asked questions about this document, something like six questions and you gave six answers to this -- to the questions that were put to you on this document. I can't help you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I will just try to ask one question. Would you look at the document. Yesterday, you testified that commanders in the field were able to use their own analysis or evaluation, or a word similar to that, in carrying out this order. Now, would you agree with me that that evaluation and analysis comes because they are following an oral order by the commander of Srebrenica, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Surely that is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To an extent, yes, but not completely, Mr. Jones. Move to another question, Ms. Sellers. We're getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could the record reflect that he is nodding his head, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. He's still looking at the document which he has seen before which he keeps saying he has never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you were asked questions on cross-examination regarding the records of Hamed Salihovic. Now, Hamed Salihovic preceded you as chief of intelligence and security. That's correct isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How did you remain in your function of chief of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 18th to 25th, but I didn't really do anything, I didn't perform any tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And including the things you didn't do, you really didn't review the records that Hamed Salihovic had left for you, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The records that he gave me, I did review and the others that he didn't give me, I would not have been able to review. Would I?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you review the working facilities that he had and the staff that worked with him, did you review their work, their input? Yes or no, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So therefore, you're not familiar with any type of secretarial or clerking assistance he might have had, in typing or drafting any of these documents, are you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: While you stated that you do know the educational level of Mr. Salihovic, you're not familiar with the educational level of the clerks or the typists or his administrative assistants, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If he had any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm asking if he -- yes, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the level of education of the clerks, the secretaries or assistant who helped Mr. Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Salihovic was a teacher. Mr. Masic was a teacher too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he have any clerical assistance that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that. I didn't know who helped whom or if there was any clerical assistance to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That exactly is what I was about to say, the witness has expressed the fact that he was not aware of any assistance, clerical assistance being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at document P143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime while the usher is finding the document, when you took over from Halilovic -- Salihovic, sorry, not Halilovic. When you took over from Salihovic, did you occupy at any time his office? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were in a small room where -- Mr. Makic resided there and I went straight to the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you never sat in the same chair that Mr. Salihovic used to sit on in his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Never. Because I remained with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That clarifies exactly his ignorance of whether there were staff, supporting staff for Mr. Salihovic. That explains the situation. Yes. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bogilovic, right now you're looking at document 143. And for sake of brevity and efficiency, I would like to say that this is a document that apparently appears to have come from commander called Zeljko Knez and the document is dated the 23rd -- I'm sorry, the 14th of October, 1992 and the content of the document relates to the reorganisation of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we be given a copy of this document. We have not received the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I just check with the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come they don't have B/C/S version of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's P143. I assumed we informed you during the break about the documents. I don't know if they're included within your documents that you have. Our apologies. I will get that for you right away. I will move on to another document in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. We were informed during the last break, but we can't always bring all the documents we have ever received from the OTP and I would like to have this one in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure there ask an extra copy. Usher, could you please hand it over to Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, my question is rather simple. Were you in receipt of this document from Commander Knez during that time period around October 14th, 1992 in that it concerns the reorganisation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the document may be removed from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to go to document 158. Mr. Bogilovic, you testified in cross-examination about the appointment of commanders. And if I understood correctly, you stated that most commanders were elected by the local population. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 99 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at the document in front of you, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please take your time and look through particularly that which comes under "order." Mr. Bogilovic, would you agree that in this document they talk about the formation of an independent group, the Glogova independent battalion, under section 1? And under section 2, it says "I hereby appoint Ejub Golic." Would you agree that that's what is written in the document, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ejub Golic had been the commander of the Glogova unit even before this. They were from Bratunac and they had their own political and military structure of the territory of Srebrenica municipality, except for the police. In the Bratunac area, the Muslim policemen were with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well then, Mr. Bogilovic, would you at least confirm that this document officially appoints him as commander of the Glogova independent battalion? And I would now draw your attention up to the top of the document, the paragraph that says: "Pursuant to article 18, paragraph 1. Isn't this his legal and official appointment?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If everything is legal, I don't know. I do not know much about the military legislation. In paragraph 2 it says I hereby appoint Ejub Golic commander of the Glogova independent battalion. But he was certainly the commander there, elected by the people, but their seat was in Srebrenica. Their headquarters. In fact -- excuse me, the name of the village escapes me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, excuse me. Then you have just testified that really you didn't know very much about military appointments that took place pursuant to the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I didn't know about this either, about this written document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can have the document removed, please. I would now like the witness to see document 155.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecutor has an extra copy, could I have the version in Bosnian, if it's available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my apologies. We will have that right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would ask you to look over the document. You have testified previously that Osman Osmanovic was the chief of staff and that he was on the military side of the organisation, Srebrenica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Osman Osmanovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this document seems to reject the appointment of Hamdija Fejzic as commander of the Bajramovici company. And if you look at the second line, what is written is that the commander of the Srebrenica independent battalion is hereby ordered to urgently appoint a commander of this unit. Are you familiar with the fact that the OS staff seems to have redirected the appointment of the commander from the Bajramovici company?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the people had elected Hamdija Fejzic the first time around as their superior, on the 1st of July, Hamdija was elected the president of the executive board and became part of the civil structures. The people again asked that Hamdija be restored to them and that's when, according to this document, Mr. Osman Osmanovic ordered that the commander of the Srebrenica independent battalion urgently appoint Bajramovic -- or rather appoint a commander, so that Hamdija would remain in the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So even though Mr. Fejzic had been appointed, elected, selected or somehow placed in the position by the people of that geographical area, the OS staff could overrule and ask that its commander appoint someone else, isn't that correct, according to this document, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in the meantime, Hamdija had performed the duty of president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Bogilovic. My question is just simply: Did Mr. Osmanovic from the OS staff, in his capacity, as chief of staff, ask that Mr. Fejzic not remain the commander and that the commander of Srebrenica appoint someone else? Yes or no, Mr. Bogilovic. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The document may be removed from the witness. I would now like to go to Defence Exhibit 238. And at the same time, I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 60, that was used in the cross-examination. I believe this was used in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the English --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to have D238 placed on the ELMO, if possible. Mr. Bogilovic, I would ask you to just briefly glance at the document. I believe that you saw it yesterday. And you confirmed that the person whose name appears at the bottom, Nedzad Bektic, is someone that you were familiar with, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Nedzad Bektic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: He's the person who succeeded you as chief of intelligence and security after you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: He wasn't the commander of the Territorial Defence to your knowledge, was he?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at Kragljevode.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. But was he the commander of the defence staff, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. He was the commander of the Kragljevode unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So he was more like a sub commander, if one could use that phrase, meaning not the top commander, but maybe a sub commander. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kragljevode, he was the top commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a leading question, Your Honours, but the witness has answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now leading questions are permissible at this stage. They weren't permissible during the examination-in-chief, but they are permissible now. Just like you in cross-examination can put leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bogilovic, if I understand you correctly, you're saying that he was the commander in his geographical area.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And he was also a member -- a member as a commander of the Territorial Defence staff, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of June, I think, that was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My question goes to section 2 of this document. I'm sorry section 1 and 2. And if I could read it into the record. This appears to be a general mobilisation order and it says: "Men between the ages of 18 and 55 are required to respond to this mobilisation and women between the ages of 18 and 50 are required to respond to this mobilisation". Are you familiar with those types of terms of or conditions of mobilisation, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What is the normal age that someone would be asked to join the army, within your understanding, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the army, I don't know. But I do know that in the police, if they were 18, they could join the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in your knowledge, do people usually join the army after 55 years old?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was a case where a child came to apply to me, asking to join the police. And I asked him, Where is your father. And he said, At home. And I said, Well, bring your father. And he brought the father and I asked the father why did you send this child to me? What can I do with the child?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is usually an age limit in terms of people serving in the army, isn't that correct, Mr. Bogilovic? An upper limit.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's in the military documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you to look at P60. You have looked at this document during your cross-examination. As was stated to you during cross-examination, this document concerns a Bogdan Zivanovic. Would you look at the first line in the first full paragraph. You confirm that it says: "Bogdan Zivanovic was born on the 14th of October, 1930 in Stublovi". Would you confirm that, Mr. Bogilovic, for the record?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't, because I don't know this man and I don't even know why this place, Stublovi is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you confirm that appears to be what is written in the document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now someone who was born in 1930, in 1993, would you agree with me that they would be about 63 years of age?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at the last full paragraph in this document. I believe this paragraph was read out to you during cross-examination. If I might read it in English translation, it says: "His", and I think we can make the assumption that "his" refers to Mr. Zivanovic, "responsibility is indisputable. Although he is outside the age bracket eligible for the regular call up, but this is just one more piece of evidence that Karadzic carried out a third call up". Would you agree that it appears that Mr. Zivanovic was older than the normal age for military recruits?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the law governing military obligations, yes. But there were people on both sides who were older and who had volunteered, but these people were all volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you agree that this is possibly a reference that a Mr. Karadzic, who is a quite well-known figure on the other side of the armed conflict on the Republika Serb side, might have had a mobilisation order that extended beyond the ages of 55 as an age limit, if you know Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. As for him and his opinions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his positions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, assuming that his position was at a certain time we'd call people over 55, this paragraph or the sentence we read out, appears to make more sense than you thought when first cross-examined. Would you agree with that, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would leave it, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Your Honour, I'm coming up to the last final documents and area. Mr. Bogilovic, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Madam Vidovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I simply wish to draw attention to the translation of this document. In this document, as in other documents of this type, the translators, for some reason, added what they thought should be included. In the Bosnian language, there is no mention of "his" not "his responsibility". Just "responsibility" is indisputable. Also in the third line, this person is -- is missing in the Bosnian text. It is not there. These documents should be checked before being used. Everything that is added by the translator alters the meaning of the document. That is why we showed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is clear enough indication in the English text that these are added by the translators. And I don't see how the meaning or the import of the original text is altered, because if there is responsibility but not his, it's certainly his responsibility that is being referred to. If it says "of no more interest" but doesn't say this person is of no more interest, it's obviously about this person that the document is talking. And later on, "little help and testified investigation, as printed," that I don't understand to be honest with you. So I don't Anyway it is not in question. Let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you worked in Srebrenica municipality for over 20 years. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber the kilometres, the miles, the distance between Potocari and the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In your estimate, how long would it take if one were in a car or any type of motor vehicle to get between Potocari and the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potocari is stretched out and it would depend from where in Potocari they're going to Srebrenica, because it stretches for 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So from the closest point, how long would it take to get between Potocari and Srebrenica, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Potocari river is -- Potocari Rijeka is halfway between Bratunac and Srebrenica and it's 5 kilometres to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How much time would it take in a motorised vehicle such as a car to get from the shortest distance from Potocari, down to Potocari to Srebrenica, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the vehicle and the driver. How fast he was driving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten, fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish it there, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next thing he will tell us is how much pressure he puts on the accelerator.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- I would like to ask you, in terms of your seeing Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much traffic there is on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- In terms of you physically seeing Naser Oric, in the fall of 1992, and in the winter of 1993, would you estimate that you saw Naser Oric more than three or four times?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you estimate also that Naser Oric was present at meetings, at least three or four times when you also were present?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you only see Naser Oric in meetings or did you have the occasion to see him outside of meetings?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely outside meetings. Anyone who was out on the ground, I would only see at the meetings I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But Naser Oric did come and visit you in the summer of 1992 and you went to Naser Oric in April of 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was then in a flat in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did he stay in the flat in Srebrenica on occasion, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that his headquarters was in Potocari, at his father's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you answer my question, please, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether Naser Oric stayed at the flat in Srebrenica on occasion?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to use document P80. Your Honour, this will be extremely brief. I do not need him to read it out, but to let you know what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you to look at document P80. We have seen it many times, in particular in connection with ERN number 02115044. In the English translation I'm referring to page 3. If you would go down numerically it says -- 1, 2, 3, and next to 3 it says "plans/actions."

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: After"plans/actions" it says "Analysis of the action, Naser." Would that conclude you to the belief that Naser Oric was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting? I cannot confirm this, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you confirm that the only person named Naser that was on the operations staff is Naser Oric? You confirmed that in your direct testimony. Can you confirm that for the Trial Chamber again?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was the only person called Naser. That was Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this meeting, if one looks above number 1, it does not have a date. It says: "Second meeting of the armed forces staff. I'm sorry. "Armed forces operation staff." If you would go to ERN number, now, that terminates in 5046, English page 4. Mr. Bogilovic, if you look under that ERN number you see "Minutes, 3rd October, 1992." Do you see where I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have some assistance about the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where it says 3 October 1992. Next to that it should say "Minutes."

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is number 4 in the English translation. It would be the part that precedes ERN number 02115046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, what page does he have in front of him?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5846. That seems to be the right page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the right page, ERN 5046?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's 5846 that I saw, not 5046. The English page, I don't know what is the corresponding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: English page, page 4, at the bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may of assistance. The Prosecutor was wrong in saying that P80 should be placed in front of the witness, because it caused confusion in our camp too. I think he is simply being shown the wrong document. So if you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could please give us the ERN number again, the one that is supposed to be please give us the ERN number again, the one that is supposed to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is P84. I'm quite grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. You've saved the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would remind Mr. Usher again: The ERN number would be on page 02115046. If you could turn to the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Again I would just simply direct Mr. Bogilovic to look at where it says 3 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And we've just testified that a Naser, Naser Oric presumably, was present at the second meeting of the armed forces operations staff. Would you agree that second meeting took place before the 3rd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to confirm the date. I can't recall the date. You have the minutes, if that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that the prior meeting then took place either in early October or sometime in September or before then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for prior to the 14th of October, there is nothing that I can confirm. The same applies to any other meetings. I can't confirm. I believe it was probably written down somewhere, but I can't just talk about it off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness now to go to -- using the same document. ERN number ends in 5489 and in the English version we have page 6. You will note there is a phrase right under that number, it says: "A meeting of the expanded staff, 7 October, Wednesday."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you see that date, 7 October, Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. It's in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would just go down to the second full line, it says, "Naser: We did all we could, but we did not manage to take out the food. How to dismantle the mines and provide protection". Would you agree that this document tends to confirm the presence of Naser Oric at the meeting on the 7th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm unable to confirm that. I don't know whether he was or whether, based on the information that he had, he confirmed. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, we'll move to the meeting of October 14th, 1992 and, Mr. Bogilovic, you testified on many occasions that you were present at that meeting. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogilovic, we've already gone over portions of that meeting where Naser Oric was reported to speak. Would you just confirm for the Trial Chamber that Naser Oric was present at the meeting on the 14th of October, 1992? That's the meeting of both the War Presidency, the operations staff and the civilian protection where you were present. Mr. Bogilovic, I believe you testified --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think most of them were actually there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to stay with document P84. I would ask the usher to go to the ERN number that ends in 5060, and in the English it is page 14. Mr. Bogilovic, do you see where it says: "Minutes of the meeting of the Srebrenica armed forces staff held on the 30th of October, 1992"?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to read down, prior to the next ERN number, prior to the number that says 5061. In the English version, it is page 15, Your Honours. I might direct your attention to the last two written lines prior to the number 5061. Would you confirm -- I'm sorry, Mr. Bogilovic, have you found where we are?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you please confirm that it says "Naser, the staff, Osman will work out the details". And then Osman concludes by saying, "The second part of the action will be without reconnaissance". Would you confirm it appears that Naser Oric was physically present at that meeting on October 30th, according to the document before you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. We might remove P84 from Mr. Bogilovic at this point. Mr. Bogilovic, you've testified that there was a person called Hazim Omerovic. Is that the correct pronunciation of his name, sir, this person who resembled Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to know, did this person ever fool you into thinking that he was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did this person ever present himself to you and say "I'm Naser Oric"?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not to me, because I knew the man's identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The persons who knew Naser Oric, such as you, you could assume that you've been fooled by the person Hazim Omerovic who looked like Naser Oric, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from close-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Hazim Omerovic riding a horse?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen Hasim horseback.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to show you a picture. It's in Sanctions now on the monitor. Mr. Bogilovic, do you recognise the person in this picture?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This person is not Hazim Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would the person in the picture ever fool you that he were Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Judge Brydensholt. One moment. One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have one very brief question that stems from Ms. Sellers' re-examination, if I may be allowed to put this one brief question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not normal that there are further questions from the Defence after the re-examination. What question do you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my understanding is that I have the right to examine a witness in redirect in case the Prosecutor touches upon something that I had no opportunity to address in my cross-examination. I would just like to ask Mr. Bogilovic about the road between Potocari and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about wartime 1992 and the first part of 1993. It is my submission that the road was -- could not be used for travel on account of the heavy and frequent shelling. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct. Many people were killed near the bend behind Camil's Cafe, because you could see the road from Zvezda, the elevation that was being used to shell the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that the staff that had your defence unit which existed before the war in March, April 1992, left during April and was present in Tuzla. Is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But as far as I understand, Srebrenica was a mixed town in the way that both Muslims and Serbs lived there before the war. Were there Serb members of this Territorial Defence unit staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did they stay in Tuzla as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that in April a Serb company came to Srebrenica and they left again, as far as I understand, in -- later in April 1992. Why did they leave Srebrenica? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They left in early May. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any fight, resistance going on before they left? Or did they just leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Akif told us, informed us when they started burning houses, he put up a defence and his cousin was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Then I understand that a lady citizen in Srebrenica went to the police -- not to you but to another policeman -- and complained that she had understood that her house was to be burned down by the Serb company. Could you tell us who was that lady? Have you any name? Was it at all in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In Srebrenica Muniba Mujic, that was the lady's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And I understand that the police officer was able to inform her that her house was not on a list of houses which were to be burned down. Is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You mentioned during your cross-examination that sometimes the War Presidency members and local commanders did something Naser Oric was not happy about. Could you give us some examples, if you know, what kind of action could that be? Where you know that Oric, who was a commander, was not happy.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first mistake he made was a protesting when Akif went on his own, without telling anyone. Akif Ustic. He left of his own accord. He should have told someone, if he had known that attacks had been carried out over there, he should have helped other people. From where his house was and on to Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Are there examples where you know that there was taking decision by members of the War Presidency which were against the will or wish of the commander?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, of course. The greatest problem was the ignorance, not knowing who was senior to whom. The staff to the Presidency, or the Presidency to the staff. That was a cause of difficulties. And logistics had to be supplied but no one was able to supply anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But you have no concrete examples, except that of Ustic, where local commanders took action against the will of Naser Oric? Well, if nothing appears to you, I have another question. You mentioned that in a meeting, I think it was on the 23rd of December, 1992, a man called Ramiz, which was a representative of the Red Cross, expressed a wish that the premises of the prison should be secured. Is that rightly understood?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Ramiz Becirovic was with the staff. Before the war, he was with the staff, too. He was not an employee of the Red Cross at any point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Why -- in what capacity or why did he ask that the premises of the prison should be secured? Had he anything to do with the prison?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation involved soldiers and, of course, if he was with the staff he had something to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: That is unclear to me. Could you try to explain that in a bit more in detail?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz, Ramiz Becirovic was a member of the staff with the army. And this probably irritated and that he should secure it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did Red Cross at all have any premises in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Red Cross, before the war, had part of that room. Another part was held by the kit man at one of the local teams, sports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Last question. In the police building, you had your offices, your premises on the first floor, whereas the military police was on the ground floor. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could it be that you had no idea whether there was a secretary or any assistance to the head of the commander of the military police before you took it over as responsible also for military police? You passed the ground floor when you visited your own police force, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was wounded on the 2nd of July, 1992. Following my leave of absence, that's when it was set up and that's when the old police station was moved into. I didn't go at first, but then later on I did pass by. But only rarely and not every day. As for secretaries, no one ever had any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I will restrict myself to one question. It was submitted to you that Naser Oric was a hero for the people who entered. You described too that the people loved Oric. They were afraid that something would happen to him. Now, what was the reason for holding Naser Oric a hero? Why have the people been afraid that he may be wounded?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only for Naser Oric's sake. It was all the commanders. They were sung by the people. Every village had a song, a hymn to praise their own commander and Naser had songs sung to his name too. As far as I'm concerned, if you ask me, my opinion is that the number 1 man should not move about as they see fit, for the sake of their own personal safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have got a final question for you before we finish. During your stay in Srebrenica, which meetings did you attend? War Presidency? Correct? Any other meetings?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings were only for the War Presidency and for the staffs. There were no other meetings, because all the decisions to be implemented by myself, the civil protection unit, the committee, the housing people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which meetings did you attend? You attended the meetings, or some of the meetings of the War Presidency. Did you attend any other meetings?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the first meeting on the 20th of May, the second meeting on the 2nd of July and the rest whenever invited by the president of the War Presidency. That's when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you attend any other meetings not of the War Presidency, but of other meetings?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because everything, all the problems were tackled by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And from your recollection, during these meetings of the War Presidency, was anyone taking minutes?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who would that person be?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, on the 20th of May, minutes were taken by Hamdija Fejzic. I believe this was also the case with the minutes of the third meeting. As for all the other meetings, that's following my return from sick leave. First Residefendic was in charge of the minutes, but then he fell ill and then another person was appointed, someone from Poljaci. The name escapes me. Nukic, that was the person's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how were the minutes kept? Were they kept in a proper minutes book? Or -- that you know of?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a notebook that was used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you describe that notebook?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a regular notebook, really. Once it was filled, they would get a new one. It wasn't always the same kind. One was bigger. One was smaller. It really depended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown again P84, please. And that is a photocopy, of course, Mr. Bogilovic. Is that familiar to you? Did you ever see that war diary or war log, call it whatever you like, before you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never. Just Mr. Nasir. He showed me some documents back then. And when I came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear: Mr. Nasir and not Mr. Naser.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. No, no. No. Nasir, Nasir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's okay. Let's not confuse it any further. So during the war you never saw that document or the original of that document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you have been referred to several pages from that document. While you were doing that, did you ever at any time recognise the handwriting on that document as belonging to someone you know?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the one that is the most familiar to me, because most of my calls came from the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic. I had no other contacts and no one sent me anything, except for three signatures. The two first ones that I saw when they were sent to me by the police, the two police officers and the third signature on the 18th of April, I had a quick look. I went through the document, and I just went on my way as soon as possible to see whether I could get anything sorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. We might be straying in the wrong direction. My understanding of your question was, you asked the witness about the War Presidency minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we've spent four days speaking at a tangent, Madam Vidovic. So be patient with me. I am going to repeat the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Your Honour, if you can please hear me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness is looking at now, I'm afraid, is something that is supposed to be the minutes of the staff and not of the War Presidency. Because this might mislead everyone. These are minutes of the staff and of their joint meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be wrong but then again, just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We asked the first questions, which meetings he attended in fact. Looking again at that document, looking at the handwriting, does that appear familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You wouldn't be in a position to tell us who could have possibly written --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That brings us to the end of your testimony. You've been here giving evidence for four days. It must have been very tiring for you. And Mr. Bogilovic, I'm sure that you are not used to this kind of testimony, long testimony, going over a weekend as well. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser and on my own behalf, and also on behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having been kind enough to come over and bear with us and give testimony for such a long time. You will receive all the assistance you require now from our staff - as soon as Mr. Usher escorts you out of the courtroom - all the preparations that are necessary to enable you to return back home will be put in place. Once more, I thank you and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May I be allowed to say something? I wish to thank you too. I wish you every success with your investigation so that justice may be restored to the extent possible. My question would be, when does my oath, my declaration cease to apply? And do you think I could possibly be allowed to greet the accused, that is my only request? I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your solemn declaration finishes here and I can't give you any authorisation to greet the accused, no. That goes beyond our jurisdiction and our powers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Once again, my thanks to all of you and my best regards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That brings us to an end. We will resume soon after, after Easter as you know. In the meantime, I have had some discussions with my legal officer and I would like you to convey to Mr. Wubben our wish that you try to articulate by the 4th of April the complete list of the witnesses that you still wish to produce, names plus what you're supposed to -- what you are expected to prove by means of these witnesses, so that we try to plan ahead with a little bit more sense and based on more information. Okay? Thank you. I know that there won't be a third session, but I -- it's my duty, my responsibility to thank all of the staff of this Trial Chamber. I wish to thank the interpreters for bearing with us and for overstaying. I wish to thank the technical staff and all of those who, security and everyone, who have been of assistance throughout the day. I thank you and I wish everyone who celebrates Easter between now and the 4th a happy Easter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.44 p.m.,
